summary: Count the subtrees of a binary tree whose nodes all have the same value.
mainInsight: Whether a subtree is uni-value depends only on its children: both child subtrees must be uni-value and each existing child must equal the node's value. A post-order DFS returns that boolean and counts the trues.
invariant: dfs(node) returns True exactly when the subtree rooted at node is uni-value, and the counter has counted every uni-value subtree inside it.

approaches.name: Check every subtree from scratch
approaches.summary: For each node, traverse its subtree comparing values.

approaches.name: Post-order DFS returning is-uni-value
approaches.summary: Children report first; the node combines their answers.
weaknesses: Must evaluate both children before combining

commonMistakes: Writing `dfs(node.left) and dfs(node.right)`, which short-circuits and skips counting in the right subtree.
Comparing the node only with the children's subtrees' flags, not their values.
Forgetting that every leaf is a uni-value subtree.
Treating a missing child as a mismatch.
edgeCases: Leaves equal to each other but not to their parent.

promptVariants: Which technique solves this problem, and what in the statement or constraints points to it?
Name the technique you would use here and the clue in the problem that tells you.
What approach fits this problem, and which part of the statement gives it away?
cards.answer: Post-order DFS where each node returns whether its subtree is uni-value. Clue: A subtree is uni-value only if all of its nodes share one value, which can be decided from the node's value and whether its two child subtrees are uni-value.
keyPoints: A subtree is uni-value only if all of its nodes share one value, which can be decided from the node's value and whether its two child subtrees are uni-value.
cards.explanation: Subtree properties that combine from children call for a post-order (bottom-up) DFS.

rubric.technique: Post-order DFS where each node returns whether its subtree is uni-value

alsoValid.name: For every node, traverse its whole subtree to check all values
alsoValid.note: correct but quadratic in the worst case

rubric.clue: A subtree is uni-value only if all of its nodes share one value, which can be decided from the node's value and whether its two child subtrees are uni-value.

promptVariants: What breaks if you write `if dfs(node.left) and dfs(node.right) and ...`?
Why must both child calls run before combining?
options: The left call would run twice
It changes the post-order into pre-order
It returns True for an empty tree twice
cards.explanation: If the left subtree is not uni-value, `and` never calls dfs(node.right), so uni-value subtrees on the right are never counted.

incorrectOptionExplanations.The left call would run twice: It runs once; the right one may not run at all.
incorrectOptionExplanations.It changes the post-order into pre-order: Order of visits is not the issue; skipped visits are.
incorrectOptionExplanations.It returns True for an empty tree twice: Empty subtrees return True once each; unrelated.

promptVariants: A root 1 with two leaf children both 2. Count?
cards.explanation: Each leaf is a uni-value subtree. The whole tree has values 1 and 2, so it is not.

promptVariants: Your code calls dfs on both children before the big if. Why does that order matter?
Explain why isLeftUni and isRightUni are computed first.
cards.answer: Both recursive calls must run so every subtree below is counted, even when one side fails. Storing them in variables first avoids the short-circuit of `and`. Then the node is uni-value if both flags are true and each existing child has the same value.
keyPoints: Then compare values of existing children
cards.explanation: Side effects inside recursive calls (here, the counter) make evaluation order important.
cards.code:
isLeftUni = dfs(root.left)
isRightUni = dfs(root.right)
if isLeftUni and isRightUni and (root.left is None or root.val == root.left.val) and (root.right is None or root.val == root.right.val):
    ans += 1
    return True
return False

promptVariants: What is the time complexity of the canonical code?
Derive the running time of the post-order DFS.
cards.explanation: Each node is visited once and does O(1) comparisons.

incorrectOptionExplanations.O(n^2): That is re-checking each subtree from scratch.

promptVariants: Recursion depth makes the space O(___).
Extra space of the DFS: O(___), the tree height.
cards.explanation: log n for a balanced tree, n for a skewed one.
